Detention Deaths, Deportation Numbers, and Systemic Violence: My Convo on The Majority Report

I joined Emma Vigeland to discuss the 16th detention death of 2026, the for-profit detention pipeline in rural Louisiana, and the latest deportation data.

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

I track ICE detention and deportation data as it's released. For the latest numbers and context: austinkocher.substack.com 

Also read: kffhealthnews.org/news/artic…

This connects directly to the detention numbers. ICE held over 70,000 people in January 2026. The children affected by those detentions don't appear in ICE's spreadsheets, but they bear real consequences.

But barriers remain. In Nevada, parents must file notarized forms with the state. Some immigrants fear government paperwork could be used to target them, a rational concern given the administration's efforts to access data across federal agencies.

California, Nevada, Maryland, New York, Virginia, and D.C. have passed laws letting parents designate temporary guardians specifically for immigration enforcement situations, keeping kids out of foster care.
An estimated 5.6 million U.S. citizen children live with a parent or family member who lacks legal immigration status. 2.6 million have two parents in that situation.

The problem: if a detained or deported parent can't appear in family court, reunification becomes far harder. Detention doesn't just separate families physically, it can sever legal custody permanently.
Oregon reported two children placed in foster care due to parental detention. The state said this had simply never happened before fall 2025. These are new consequences of enforcement at this scale.

Parents of 11,000 U.S. citizen children were detained between January and August 2025, per ProPublica. At least 32 children ended up in foster care across seven states. Advocates say the real number is likely much higher.

As ICE detention hit record highs this year, states started asking an urgent question: what happens to the children of detained parents? Several states are now rewriting custody laws in response. A thread.

I’m excited to share that I’ll be giving a virtual talk on Tuesday, April 21st from 5:30 to 7:00 PM Eastern via Zoom, hosted by the School of Social and Behavioral Sciences at Mercy University. 

Join Here:buff.ly/0hcS3iP
All data from ICE's own biweekly releases. Full breakdown with charts, sourcing, and context in my latest post: austinkocher.substack.com/p/…
Since January 2025, 47 people have died in ICE custody. In 2026 alone: 16 deaths, that's 1 every 6.3 days. At this pace, 2026 would exceed 60 custody deaths for the year.

Book-ins tell a clear story about who's driving enforcement now. CBP used to contribute up to 485 people/day to ICE detention. By March 2026: just 94/day. ICE interior arrests now account for 91% of all book-ins.

The administration says it targets dangerous criminals. The data says otherwise: 73% of ICE detainees have no criminal conviction. Only 5% have a violent conviction. People with no criminal history remain the largest detained group.
Where did the decline come from? Mostly a 21% drop in detentions of people with no criminal record. That shift followed the backlash after ICE agents shot and killed two civilians in Minneapolis.
ICE's detained population hit a record 70,766 in late January, then dropped 15% to 60,311 by April 4. But 60,311 is still higher than any pre-Trump II figure on record.
At the current pace, FY2026 is on track for over 460,000 removals. That's still less than half the administration's stated goal of 1 million per year.
ICE averaged 1,286 deportations per day through April 4. The first half of FY2026: 234,236 removals, 74% more than the same period in either of the two prior fiscal years.
ICE published new detention data after a 56-day gap, the longest reporting blackout since Trump took office. Here's what the numbers show. A thread with charts. 🧵
